newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says Italy will not seek EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says Italy will not seek EMU delay.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Thursday ruled out seeking a delay to the start of Europe's planned monetary union and announced new steps to help convince Italy's partners that it would be ready to join.

Speaking in the Senate (upper house), Prodi repeated his commitment to meet the strict economic terms for founder membership in January 1999, saying he had "signed a pact with the Italian people" to keep the country at the forefront of Europe.
"Italy will not ask for a delay or easy terms. Italy is in a condition to undergo the test that all European countries have to undergo for the single currency," Prodi said.

He was speaking hours after the man whose party ensures the centre-left government's survival, Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti, called for a negotiated delay to the start of economic and monetary union (EMU).

Bertinotti told state radio RAI that Italy "in concert with the other European countries, should advance a realistic proposal of elasticity, at least in terms of the Maastricht criteria and an extension of the time-scale".
Refoundation is vital to Prodi since its votes in the lower house of parliament ensure the government's majority.

It is opposed to any cuts in spending or tax hikes in a 1997 mini-budget Prodi is preparing to meet the tough deficit test for EMU and has threatened to withdraw support if the government does a deal with the opposition on an early 1998 budget.

Prodi's political headaches are matched by scepticism in some EU countries, notably Germany, about whether Italy can meet the EMU criteria in 1997, the key year for consideration for founder membership, or sustain them once in the currency club.
Prodi told the Senate that his government would seek to reassure financial markets and EU partners by issuing "extremely detailed" economic targets for 1998 to 2000 by May 15.
The three-year targets, contained in a document known as the DPEF, set out the framework for the 1998 budget and will point to how Italy intends to sustain adherence to the EMU rules.

"With or without an agreement between the government and the opposition (on bringing forward the 1998 budget) the government intends to send a clear message to our European partners and to the markets," Prodi said.

Prodi earlier spoke by telephone with French President Jacques Chirac and a French spokesman said both leaders had reaffirmed their determination to see their countries join the new currency, the Euro, at the planned date.

French sources said Chirac had above all sought to reassure Prodi in the half-hour conversation that France and Germany were not discussing any deal behind Rome's back to delay Italian membership of the planned single European currency.

The Italian government has been ultra-sensitive to any suggestion that it might not qualify for the first wave of member countries, although economists doubt its chances of bringing its public sector deficit down to the required three percent of gross domestic product, from 6.8 percent last year.
Prodi told the Senate that the EMU drive, a stimulus for Italy to end its record of profligate deficit spending, would help make the country "modern, credible and efficient".
Missing founder membership, he said, would make it "extremely difficult to catch up for lost time later".
"Experience teaches us that, once formed, a club sets increasingly exclusive norms to protect its own members, making it ever more difficult for new associates to be admitted."
